newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, bonds rise, dollar falls.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, bonds rise, dollar falls.

text.p: Stock and bond investors had a little party Friday after Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan appeared to back away from favouring another rise in short-term interest rates. But the dollar took a beating.
Gold rose, and oil edged higher.
The Dow Jones industrial average rose 32.91 points to 7,169.53, a day after jumping 51 points on a proposed cut in the capital gains tax.
In the broader market, advancing issues beat declines 1,525 to 933 on moderate volume of 455 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
Investors struggled early in the session to divine the Fed's next move after Greenspan's speech in New York late on Thursday.
Bond prices moved higher but stocks were erratic as Wall Street again found nothing conclusive in the the central bank chief's comments.

"I think people can read whatever it is they wanted to in his comments," said Peter Canelo, chief investment strategist at Dean Witter. "He did allude to some good things happening but there was really nothing new here."
Indeed, it seemed Greenspan's speech included at least one warning to offset every piece of good news.

He spent much of the speech defending the Fed's March interest rate increase, pointing to the need for the central bank to act pre-emptively against inflation risks. But he also cast some doubt whether such a need existed now.
"To be sure, 1997 is not 1994 when the Fed was forced to tighten monetary conditions very substantially to avoid accommodating rising inflation," Greenspan said.
It was in 1994 and early 1995 that the Fed raised short-term rates seven times, doubling rates to 6 percent from 3 percent in the process.

While analysts were divided on whether the Fed will pause before moving again, many argue that regardless of the next move, the stock market's recent rebound has taken prices to a level where risks likely outweigh rewards over the near term.
The Fed raised short-term interest rates a quarter point on March 25, the first increase in more than two years.

In the bond market, prices shot higher, with the benchmark 30-year Treasury up 17/32, or $5.31 on a $1,000 bond, lowering its yield to 6.89 percent from 6.94 percent on Thursday. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
"We're definitely cautious here," said Philip Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management. "The risk right now is to the downside rather than to the upside."

With wholesale and retail price, industrial production and housing starts reports all due next week and the Fed's May 20 meeting drawing closer, analysts said the stock and bond markets would likely resume their choppy pattern.
In currency trading, the dollar fell to 120.20 Japanese yen late in New York from 123.75 late on Thursday and to 1.6875 German marks from 1.7085.

Until this week, the dollar had been supported by expectations of higher U.S. rates and continued low rates in Japan. Higher rates tend to bolster a country's currency by making its bonds and other assets relatively more attractive.
But Greenspan's speech and a Japanese newspaper report hinting at higher rates in Japan led traders to re-evaluate these rate expectations and send the dollar lower.
Meanwhile, gold rose sharply, boosted by the dollar's weakness. Gold for June delivery rose $4.50 to $349.30 an ounce on New York's Commodity Exchange.
June crude oil added 9 cents to $20.43 a barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 rose 50.5 points to 4,630.9, a rise of 175.3 points for the week, and Toyko's Nikkei average fell 259.03 points to 19,802.78 but was up 288.03 from last week.
